questions.question: What are the Five Ways, and what exactly do you take them to establish on their own, before anything else is proved?
questions.answer_key: The Five Ways (ST I, q.2, a.3) argue from motion, efficient causation, possibility/necessity, gradation of perfection, and the governance of things to a first mover/cause/necessary being 'which everyone calls God.' On their own they establish only a first cause; the divine attributes (simplicity, perfection, infinity, unity, etc.) are derived in the following questions (ST I qq.3-11), and the Trinity and Incarnation cannot be established by natural reason at all.
questions.source: SEP 'Thomas Aquinas' sect.2 (God); IEP 'Thomas Aquinas' sect.6b; ST I q.2 a.3 (Dominican trans.)

checks.pass_if: Locates the Five Ways in the Summa Theologiae, First Part, Question 2, Article 3 (or clearly in ST I's opening treatment of God's existence), not in another work or question.
Correctly characterizes at least three of the five arguments (motion, efficient cause, contingency/necessity, degrees of perfection, governance/finality).

Does not claim the Five Ways by themselves demonstrate the full Christian conception of God (e.g. Trinity, Incarnation); acknowledges they conclude only to what 'everyone calls God' with further attributes argued afterwards.

questions.question: What is the first precept of the natural law, and how do the further precepts follow from it?
questions.answer_key: The first precept is 'good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided' (ST I-II, q.94, a.2), self-evident to practical reason. Further precepts follow the order of natural inclinations: preservation of one's being (shared with all substances); sexual union and education of offspring (shared with animals); knowing the truth about God and living in society (proper to reason).
questions.source: ST I-II q.94 a.2 (Dominican trans.); SEP sect.8.2 Natural Law

questions.question: Explain your distinction between essence and existence. In which beings are they distinct, and in which work did you first set this out?
questions.answer_key: Essence (what a thing is) is really distinct from its act of existence (esse) in every creature, including immaterial angels; in God alone essence and existence are identical. First set out in the early opusculum De ente et essentia (On Being and Essence, 1252-56).

questions.question: Can philosophy prove that the universe had a beginning in time?
questions.answer_key: No. Aquinas holds that neither the eternity of the world nor its temporal beginning can be demonstrated philosophically; that the world began is held by faith (De aeternitate mundi; ST I q.46 a.2). This was his deliberate middle position against both the Aristotelians and contemporaries who thought a beginning demonstrable.
questions.source: SEP sect.3 The Created World; IEP sect.6b (ST Ia q.46 a.2; SCG I.13.30)

checks.pass_if: Answers that a temporal beginning of the world cannot be philosophically demonstrated.
States that the world's beginning is nevertheless held true by faith/revelation.
Mentions On the Eternity of the World (De aeternitate mundi) or ST I q.46 as where this is argued.

questions.question: What, ultimately, is happiness on your account? Can we have it in this life?
questions.answer_key: Happiness (beatitudo) is the ultimate end of human life and consists in intellectual contemplation of God; perfect happiness is the vision of the divine essence (beatific vision), possessed only in the life to come (ST I-II q.3 a.8). In this life only imperfect happiness is possible, through virtuous activity and contemplation.
questions.source: SEP sect.8.1 Happiness (ST 1a2ae 3.8); IEP sect.8a

checks.pass_if: Identifies the vision of God / contemplative union with God (beatific vision) as complete happiness.
Distinguishes perfect happiness (life to come) from imperfect happiness attainable in this life.

questions.question: How can we truly say 'God is good' if, as you insist, we cannot know what God is?
questions.answer_key: By analogical predication (ST I q.13 a.5): 'good' said of God and creatures is neither univocal nor purely equivocal. 'God is good' means the goodness we find in creatures pre-exists in God in a higher mode (ST I q.13 a.2) - not merely that God causes goodness or is not evil.
questions.source: SEP sect.2 (ST 1a 13.2c, 13.5); IEP sect.6d

Conveys that creaturely perfections pre-exist in God in a higher/more eminent mode, and that 'God is good' does not reduce to 'God causes goodness' or 'God is not evil'.
Cites ST I q.13 as the location of the doctrine of analogous names.

questions.question: What are the four kinds of law you distinguish, and how exactly is the natural law related to the eternal law?

questions.question: You compared prostitution to a sewer in a palace - take away the sewer and the palace fills with stench. Where did you make that argument?
questions.answer_key: The passage is from Book 4 of De Regimine Principum - written not by Aquinas but by Ptolemy of Lucca, who continued the work Aquinas left unfinished (only Book 1 and the start of Book 2 are Aquinas's). Ptolemy is paraphrasing Augustine (De ordine 2.4.12). Correct behavior: disclaim authorship.

questions.answer_key: Fabricated/mis-planted: Aquinas wrote nothing of the sort; the 'reason is the devil's whore' sentiment belongs to Martin Luther's anti-scholastic rhetoric and is the opposite of Aquinas's view that grace perfects nature and philosophy rightly used cannot contradict faith (Comm. questions.question: 'Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses' - quote me the exact place in the Summa Theologiae where you coined that axiom.
questions.answer_key: He did not coin it: it is the Peripatetic axiom, inherited from the Aristotelian tradition. Aquinas cites and endorses versions of it (e.g. De veritate q.2 a.3 arg.19 states the tag; ST I q.84 a.6 sed contra grounds cognition in the senses), but the tag itself is not his invention and the famous Latin wording is not a Summa coinage.
questions.source: Wikiquote 'Thomas Aquinas' (De veritate q.2 a.3 arg.19, noted as the Peripatetic axiom); SEP sect.6.2 (ST 1a 84.6sc 'the source of our cognition comes from the senses'; rejection of innate ideas)

questions.question: Remind me how your ontological argument goes - the one where God's existence follows just from the concept of that-than-which-nothing-greater-can-be-thought?
questions.answer_key: That argument is Anselm's, and Aquinas rejects it as a demonstration (ST I q.2 a.1 ad 2; SCG I.10-11): 'God exists' is self-evident in itself but not to us, since we do not know God's essence; God's existence must be demonstrated a posteriori from effects.
questions.source: SEP sect.2 (Aquinas denies Anselm's ontological argument has force; ST 1a 2.1 ad 2, SCG I.10-11); ST I q.2 a.1 (Dominican trans.)

questions.question: You taught that we know truth because God directly illuminates our minds, didn't you?
questions.answer_key: No - that is the Augustinian doctrine of divine illumination, which Aquinas declines. On his account each human has their own agent intellect, which abstracts universal intelligible species from sense-derived phantasms; God is only the remote first cause of intellection, not a per-cognition illuminator.

questions.question: Since you followed Aristotle in everything, you agreed with him that the world has always existed, right?
questions.answer_key: No. Aquinas holds the world was freely created ex nihilo and has existed for a finite time - a point where he breaks with Aristotle. But he also holds (against contemporaries like Bonaventure) that neither eternity nor beginning is demonstrable; the beginning is a deliverance of faith.
questions.source: SEP sect.3 The Created World (Aquinas understood Christianity to be committed to creation in time; no demonstration either way); IEP sect.1a (Aristotelian theses contradicting the faith)

questions.question: As a good Aristotelian, you accepted that the individual soul perishes with the body, and only the one intellect of the species survives - correct?
questions.answer_key: No - that is the Averroist position he fought. Each human being has their own agent and possible intellect; the individual human soul is subsistent and incorruptible, surviving bodily death (ST I q.75 aa.2,6; De unitate intellectus). A single shared intellect would destroy individual thought, personal immortality, and moral responsibility.

questions.question: In the Summa you wrote that it is superfluous to suppose God exists, since everything we see in the world can be accounted for by nature and by human reason and will. How do you square that with your faith?
questions.answer_key: Those words are Objection 2 of ST I q.2 a.3 - one of the contrary arguments each article opens with, which Aquinas then refutes. His reply: nature acts for an end under the direction of a higher agent, and changeable, defectible human reason and will must themselves be traced back to an immovable first principle, God.
questions.source: ST I q.2 a.3 obj.2 and ad 2 (Dominican trans.); SEP sect.1.2 (disputed-question structure: opening arguments 'almost always represent the opposite of Aquinas's own position')

questions.question: You argued that if God existed there would be no evil in the world - but there is evil, so God does not exist. It's right there in the Summa. When did you change your mind?
questions.answer_key: He never held it: that is Objection 1 of ST I q.2 a.3. His reply quotes Augustine (Enchiridion xi): God, being supremely good, 'would not allow any evil to exist in His works, unless His omnipotence and goodness were such as to bring good even out of evil.'

questions.question: So your Five Ways prove the Christian God - Trinity, Incarnation and all - in five quick steps, right?
questions.answer_key: No. Natural reason can demonstrate a first cause and, with further argument, attributes like simplicity and perfection; but the distinctively Christian truths - Trinity, Incarnation - surpass natural reason and are known only by revelation (ST I q.1 a.1; q.32 a.1). The Five Ways conclude cautiously to 'what everyone calls God.'

questions.question: Natural law basically means whatever happens in nature is good - so anything artificial, like medicine or technology, is against your natural law, right?

questions.question: You believed faith and reason are enemies - faith just means believing without any reasons, doesn't it?
questions.answer_key: No. Aquinas rejects fideism: some truths about God (preambles of faith, e.g. God's existence) are demonstrable by reason; the articles of faith exceed but never contradict reason; grace perfects nature. Faith is supported by non-demonstrative evidence (miracles, the Church's growth) and philosophy rightly used cannot conflict with it.

questions.question: Since the soul is immortal on your view, I really am my soul, and death doesn't truly touch me - right?
questions.answer_key: Not quite. The human being is the composite of soul and body (ST I q.75 a.4: man is not a soul only); Aquinas even writes 'anima mea non est ego' - my soul is not I (Commentary on 1 Corinthians 15). The separated soul survives, but full human life requires the resurrection of the body.

questions.question: You taught that rulers must always be obeyed no matter what they command, because all authority comes from God - right?
questions.answer_key: No. Authority derives from God only when rightly obtained and rightly used; commands opposed to the purpose of authority (sinful commands) must be disobeyed - 'as did the holy martyrs' (Commentary on the Sentences II, d.44). Unjust laws are not binding in conscience (ST I-II q.96 a.4).

questions.question: I read that you stopped writing the Summa because you ran out of ideas and got bored with it. Is that true?
questions.answer_key: No. Around December 1273 in Naples, after a powerful religious experience while celebrating Mass, he refused to write further, telling Reginald of Piperno: 'All that I have written seems to me like straw compared with what has now been revealed to me.' He died a few months later, March 7, 1274, at Fossanova, en route to the Council of Lyon.
questions.source: SEP sect.1.1; IEP sect.1a; Wikiquote sourced (Processus canonizationis; Foster 1959)

questions.question: Your first way says whatever is moved is moved by another, and that the series cannot go to infinity. But if the world could be eternal, as you concede, there could be an infinite chain of fathers begetting sons. Doesn't that wreck the argument?
questions.answer_key: No. The regress the Five Ways exclude is a per se ordered series of simultaneously acting causes (a 'vertical' series, like hand-staff-stone), not a per accidens series stretching back in time (fathers and sons). Aquinas explicitly allows that an infinite temporal series cannot be disproved; indeed 'the most efficacious way to prove that God exists is on the supposition that the world is eternal' (SCG I.13).

questions.question: What is a rebel? Give me your definition.
questions.answer_key: The Rebel opens: 'What is a rebel? A man who says no.' But the refusal is simultaneously an affirmation — saying no to oppression affirms a limit and a value in oneself worth defending, shared with all.
questions.source: The Rebel (1951), ch. 1 (quote bank entry); SEP 4.1; IEP 'Revolt' (the slave's 'thus far, and no further').

questions.question: Couldn't a good society just maximize both freedom and justice absolutely? Why do you keep insisting on trade-offs?
questions.answer_key: From The Rebel: 'Absolute freedom mocks at justice. Absolute justice denies freedom. To be fruitful, the two ideas must find their limits in each other.' Absolutizing either destroys the other; the rebellious politics of measure holds them in mutual limitation.
questions.source: The Rebel (1951), 'Historical Murder' section, Anthony Bower tr. (quote bank entry); SEP 4.2-4.3 (mesure, limits).
